0.0.n: Introduces what the speaker wants to keep visually simple.

0.1.n: Marks ノート as the topic of the sentence.

0.2.n: Used with a negative form to mean not very or not excessively.

0.3.n: This borrowed adjective describes the appearance of the notes.

0.4.n: Links カラフル to する, expressing how the notes are made.

0.5.n: せず is a negative linking form of する, equivalent here to しないで.

0.7.n: 色 counts colors here; 3色 is read さんしょく.

0.8.n: Sets three colors as the maximum allowed.

0.9.n: Marks the content of the decision: a maximum of three colors.

0.10.n: The て-form of 決める links setting the limit to organizing the notes.

0.11.n: Here it refers to where the study material is written and organized.

0.12.n: Marks the notebook as the destination for the organized material.

0.13.n: まとめる + ています politely describes the speaker’s regular note-taking practice.

1.0.n: Japanese does not mark plural here; the context suggests several pens of different colors.

1.1.n: Marks ペン as what is used excessively.

1.2.n: The stem of 使う plus すぎる expresses excessive use.

1.3.n: Introduces a condition whose usual consequence follows.

1.5.n: The past form of 色分けする modifies 意味 and 目的: the point and purpose of having color-coded.

1.6.n: Here it means the significance or rationale behind color-coding.

1.7.n: Links related examples without presenting them as a complete list.

1.8.n: Refers to what the color-coding is intended to achieve.

1.9.n: Marks 意味や目的 as what becomes hard to understand.

1.10.n: 分かる + づらい expresses difficulty; づらく is the linking form used before なる.

1.11.n: Expresses a change toward being difficult to understand.

1.12.n: Turns the preceding statement into a noun-like unit that can be linked to another reason.

1.13.n: Connects this problem with the additional reason explained in the next line.

2.0.n: Introduces the writing tools whose colors receive too much attention.

2.1.n: Connects ペン to カラー, identifying whose colors are being discussed.

2.2.n: This borrowed noun refers to pen colors; the wording around カラー意図 is compressed and somewhat awkward.

2.3.n: Refers to the intended significance assigned to the different pen colors.

2.4.n: Links intentions and purposes as related, non-exhaustive examples.

2.5.n: Refers to the different functions assigned to pen colors.

2.6.n: Marks the intentions and purposes as what increase in number.

2.7.n: The linking form of 多い combines with なる to describe an increase.

2.8.n: With 多く, it indicates that the number grows.

2.9.n: Presents having more color-related purposes as the condition leading to distraction.

2.11.n: Points back to managing the pen colors and their purposes, rather than a physical place.

2.12.n: Marks the target toward which attention turns.

2.13.n: Here it means mental focus rather than consciousness in the medical sense.

2.14.n: Marks 意識 as what turns toward the color system.

2.15.n: 向く + てしまう suggests an unwanted result; the final て links it to what follows.

2.16.n: Combines with 内容 to specify the material being learned.

2.17.n: Together with 勉強, it refers to the actual subject matter.

2.18.n: Marks the study material as what fails to sink in.

2.19.n: 入る + てくる is negative here; material not coming in metaphorically means not being absorbed mentally.

2.20.n: Introduces the reason for the simple note-taking approach described next.

3.0.n: This borrowed adjective describes the desired style of the notes.

3.1.n: Links シンプル to する to express making or keeping something that way.

3.2.n: The stem of する attaches to ながら; the notes are the implied object.

3.3.n: Attaches to a verb stem to show two actions happening together.

3.5.n: Places the future review after the initial note-taking.

3.6.n: The past form modifies 時, presenting reviewing as completed at that point, even though the occasion is future.

3.7.n: After a verb, 時 identifies the occasion when that action happens.

3.8.n: Marks 振り返った時 as the occasion for finding the notes easy to read.

3.9.n: 見る + やすい expresses ease; やすく links this description to なる.

3.10.n: Describes the desired result of making the notes visually accessible.

3.11.n: Together with に, it introduces the desired outcome rather than a comparison.

3.12.n: Completes ように, marking ease of later review as the goal.

3.13.n: Connects the preceding goal to こと, presenting it as an idea the speaker keeps in mind.

3.14.n: Turns the stated goal into something that can be the object of 意識する.

3.15.n: Marks the goal as what the speaker consciously keeps in mind.

3.16.n: The て-form of 意識する links conscious attention to the act of writing.

3.17.n: A conversational contraction of 書いています, retaining politeness and describing the speaker’s usual practice.

0.lit: As for notes, without making them too colorful, deciding on up to three colors, I organize them in a notebook.
0.tip: せず means without doing and links the negative action to the rest of the sentence.

1.lit: If you overuse pens, the point and purpose of having color-coded become hard to understand, and
1.tip: The final のと packages this whole problem as one item and connects it to another reason.

2.lit: When pen-color intentions and purposes increase, attention ends up turning there, and study content does not come in, so
2.tip: 入ってこない literally means does not come in, but here describes study material failing to sink in.

3.lit: While keeping it simple, I write mindful of the idea: so it becomes easy to read when looking back later.
3.tip: ように expresses the desired outcome: making the notes easy to read during later review.
